analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: 2027 Consumer Outlook: Steady Through the Shocks
key_insights: GS estimates US consumer spending rises 2.5% in 2026 (Q4/Q4), driven by strong Q2 and Q3 growth when larger tax refunds from the OBBBA and equity-market wealth effects more than offset the drag from higher energy prices after the Iran war began.

2026 growth reflects solid services demand, a rebound in durables spending after tariff-driven price increases cooled demand in late 2025, and a temporary boost from election-related nonprofit spending ahead of the midterms.
Households drew down savings to absorb the energy shock. The saving rate has fallen about 1.5pp since the start of the year to a measured 3.8%.
GS forecasts consumer spending growth of 2.2% in 2027 (Q4/Q4), close to its estimate of potential and modestly above consensus.
Real disposable income is forecast to rise only 1.4% in 2026 (Q4/Q4) because higher inflation was not matched by faster wage growth. GS expects 2.3% in 2027.

The 2027 income pickup comes mostly from a fading inflation drag as tariff, energy and AI-related price impulses abate. Higher net interest income (households are net lenders in aggregate) and 3.6% Social Security and transfer COLAs also contribute. Labor compensation contributes about as much as in 2026.

Real income growth was uneven in 2026. Medicaid and SNAP cuts and gasoline costs hit lower-income households hardest, and the lowest income quintile spends about four times as much on gasoline as a share of after-tax income as the top quintile. Slower nominal wage growth for lower-income workers added to the gap. Middle- and higher-income households captured most of the OBBBA tax-refund boost.
GS expects real income growth to be more evenly spread across income quintiles in 2027 as inflation eases, wage growth converges, and COLAs lift transfer-reliant lower-income households.

GS expects Democrats to win concessions in the government funding and debt limit negotiations, likely a partial reversal of the Medicaid and SNAP cuts and possibly reinstatement of the enhanced ACA health insurance subsidies. This would support income at the low end.
Household net worth as a share of disposable income is near its all-time high, though the gains have gone disproportionately to higher-income and higher-wealth households.

GS puts the saving rate at about 5%, roughly 1pp above the published 3.8%, after adjusting for downward retail sales revisions that official income and spending data will not incorporate until next year. GS also thinks personal interest income is understated, though it is less confident that gap will be revised away.

A low saving rate fits the current backdrop of near-record net worth and a balanced labor market. GS expects the published rate to edge down to about 3.5% over the next few months, then move sideways, and be revised up in late 2027.
Household debt-to-income and debt service ratios have edged lower in recent months, and mortgage and consumer credit delinquencies have declined.

The GS baseline has the Fed delivering a final hike in December and resuming cuts in late 2027 or early 2028. Higher rates subtract about 0.2pp from 2027 consumption growth through weaker credit-financed durables demand, concentrated in motor vehicles and recreation goods.

GS expects a softer start to 2027. The rate drag on durables peaks in Q2, energy prices stay elevated through Q1, and nonprofit election spending pays back (roughly a 0.2pp drag on annualized growth if normalization completes by Q1). Growth then picks up as inflation falls, tax refunds arrive and benefit cuts partly reverse.

GS sees risks to the 2027 consumption forecast tilted modestly to the downside. Wealth effects added over 0.4pp to 2026 growth and should add about 0.2pp in 2027 in the baseline, and less if AI-related stocks keep falling. Risks to the disinflation forecast are on the upside, most obviously from energy.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Resilient consumer despite the energy price spike, helped by tax refunds and equity gains in Q2 and Q3.
Near-potential pace, slower than 2026, modestly above consensus, with a softer first half and a pickup later in the year.
Weak because inflation, mainly energy, outpaced wage growth.
Pickup from disinflation, higher net interest income and COLAs supports spending.
Low measured rate, but GS argues it is understated and not a warning sign given strong balance sheets.
GS estimate after adjusting for retail sales revisions, about 1pp above the published figure.
GS expects a small further decline in the published rate as households absorb energy costs, then flat, then revised up in late 2027.
Boosts real income, most for lower-income households that rely on transfers.

macro_indicators.reading: final hike in December 2026, cuts resume late 2027/early 2028
macro_indicators.interpretation: Higher rates cut 2027 consumption growth by about 0.2pp via durables demand.

risk_factors: Fading wealth effects: they added over 0.4pp to 2026 spending growth and should add about 0.2pp in 2027, less if AI-related stocks continue to decline.
Upside inflation risk, mainly from energy, from any current or new shock, which would further weigh on real disposable income.
Higher interest rates weigh on credit-financed durables demand (about 0.2pp drag in 2027).
Payback from election-related nonprofit spending after the midterms (about 0.2pp drag on annualized growth early in 2027).
The saving rate gap may not be fully revised away, because the interest income understatement may reflect measurement difficulty.
charts_described: Exhibit 7 shows the published personal saving rate at 3.8% in September 2026 against a GS-adjusted 4.9%, with the adjustment reflecting annual revisions to retail sales.
Exhibit 10 compares GS and consensus real PCE growth forecasts, with GS at 2.2% for 2027 on a Q4/Q4 basis, modestly above consensus.
geopolitical: The Iran war and the resulting energy price spike weighed on 2026 real incomes and consumer spending.
Energy prices are expected to stay elevated through Q1 2027, with upside inflation risk from any current or new energy shock.
